newsitem.title: UK: Britain revives war tribute after 60 years.
newsitem.headline: Britain revives war tribute after 60 years.

text.p: Millions of people in shops, offices, factories, stations and airports throughout Britain observed a two-minute silence to honour the country's war dead on Monday in the first such weekday tribute since the 1930s.

The tribute, proposed by veterans eager to maintain the remembrance tradition as the years pass, came at 11 o'clock on the eleventh day of the eleventh month -- the time of the 1918 armistice that ended World War One.

The tradition had been abandoned before World War Two and replaced by an annual remembrance ceremony on the closest Sunday to Armistice Day. This was led on Sunday by Queen Elizabeth, again with the revival of two-minute silences in many public places.
A spokesman for the Royal British Legion veterans' association hailed the success of its campaign, backed by major companies and public institutions.

"What today allows people to do is to stop for just a couple of minutes and pause during the workday life to remember why it is they are here and how it is they are here, and just to reflect on the freedom they are enjoying today," he said.
Thousands of ex-servicemen and school children wearing the paper poppies that symbolise the Commonwealth war dead joined the silent tribute.
"They say the good die young, and they did," one first world war ex-serviceman said.
In France, President Jacques Chirac laid a wreath on the tomb of France's Unknown Soldier, commemorating the 78th anniversary of the day German forces accepted an armistice ending four years of war.
Thousands of similar ceremonies took place thoughout France.

Virtually every one of France's 35,000 towns and villages had a war monument erected after World War One with the names of local dead inscribed upon it and flowers were laid there at ceremonies on Monday, as they had on Sunday in Britain.
An opinion poll suggests strong feeling in France as well as Britain that the day should continue to be marked. About 87 percent questioned in a survey in France backed the tradition.
But Monday's ceremonies in Paris were not without controversy.

A group of some 15 anti-AIDS militants who gathered near official ceremonies tried to disrupt proceedings by sounding fog horns and unfurling banners accusing government of indifference to AIDS sufferers. They were quickly led away by police.
